title: Spinal Cord Anatomy: Gray Horns, White Tracts & Pathway
description: Master spinal cord anatomy in cross-section and length, from dorsal sensory and ventral motor roots to gray matter horns, white tracts, and spinal segment.
h1: Spinal Cord Anatomy: Gray Matter Horns, White Tracts and Roots
blurb: Protected inside the vertebral canal, a butterfly core of gray-matter neuron horns is surrounded by ascending sensory and descending motor white-matter tracts.
lead: Running through the protective tunnel of the vertebral column, the spinal cord is a two-way superhighway linking the brain with every trunk and limb segment. In this illustrated guide to spinal cord anatomy, we examine 22 documented structures—including posterior (dorsal) horn, anterior (ventral) horn, lateral horn, central canal—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Running through the protective tunnel of the vertebral column, the spinal cord is a two-way superhighway linking the brain with every trunk and limb segment. In cross-section the cord shows an H- or butterfly-shaped core of grey matter — posterior (sensory) horns, lateral (autonomic) horns in thoracic segments and anterior (motor) horns — around the central canal. White matter surrounds it in funiculi carrying the dorsal column–medial lemniscus (fine touch, proprioception), the spinothalamic tracts (pain, temperature) and the corticospinal tracts (voluntary movement). Dorsal roots carry sensory fibres with their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion; ventral roots carry motor fibres. Three meninges and the denticulate ligaments suspend the cord in CSF. Within the human body, the spinal cord (Medulla spinalis) is situated in vertebral canal, foramen magnum to L1/L2, receives arterial perfusion via anterior spinal artery + two posterior, reinforced by radicular arteries, and is innervated by 31 pairs of spinal nerves; ascending & descending tracts.

The posterior (dorsal) horn (Cornu posterius) is the slender upper horns receiving sensory afferents; laminae I–VI including the substantia gelatinosa. Physiologically, the posterior (dorsal) horn governs first synapse for pain, temperature and touch; gate control of nociception happens here. The anterior (ventral) horn (Cornu anterius) is the broad lower horns containing the lower motor neuron cell bodies and Renshaw cells. Physiologically, the anterior (ventral) horn governs final common pathway: alpha motor neurons innervate skeletal muscle. Structurally, the lateral horn (Cornu laterale) comprises present only in T1–L2, holding preganglionic sympathetic neurons (and S2–S4 parasympathetic equivalents). Physiologically, the lateral horn governs origin of the sympathetic outflow. The central canal (Canalis centralis) is the ependyma-lined remnant of the neural tube lumen, continuous with the fourth ventricle. Physiologically, the central canal governs circulates a trickle of CSF within the cord. Structurally, the white funiculi & tracts (Funiculi) comprises dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis & cuneatus), lateral spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts. Physiologically, the white funiculi & tracts governs highways for sensation upward and motor commands downward. The dura mater is the tough outer sleeve, ending as the dural sac at S2 with the filum terminale beyond. Physiologically, the dura mater protects and forms the epidural and subarachnoid boundaries.

Clinically, regarding the posterior (dorsal) horn, loss of the spinothalamic decussation at a segment causes a segmental band of lost pain and temperature (syringomyelia). From a diagnostic standpoint, in the anterior (ventral) horn, poliovirus and ALS destroy these cells, giving flaccid paralysis, wasting and fasciculation. In clinical pathology involving the lateral horn, horner syndrome follows interruption of the T1 lateral horn or its pathway (e.g. Pancoast tumour). Medical evaluation of the central canal also notes that its dilatation defines syringomyelia, classically causing a cape-like loss of pain and temperature.

questions.question: Where does the spinal cord end in adults?
questions.answer: In most adults, the spinal cord ends as the conus medullaris near the L1–L2 vertebral level; nerve roots continue below as the cauda equina.

questions.question: What is the difference between gray and white matter in the spinal cord?
questions.answer: Central gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies and local circuits; surrounding white matter carries ascending sensory and descending motor pathways.

questions.question: What is the posterior (dorsal) horn?
questions.answer: The posterior horn is the dorsal gray-matter region of the spinal cord that receives and processes sensory afferents.

questions.question: Where is the lateral horn located?
questions.answer: The lateral horn is in the spinal gray matter, most distinctly at thoracic and upper lumbar levels (classically T1–L2).

questions.question: What is the function of the white funiculi & tracts?
questions.answer: Spinal white-matter tracts carry sensory information upward and motor commands downward between the body and brain.
